title: Pyrethroid Resistance in Nigeria: How Chlorfenapyr Mosquito Nets Work
excerpt: Nigeria's mosquitoes are surviving pyrethroids. Here's what chlorfenapyr nets actually change.
author: Harvestfield Healthcare
body:
Pyrethroid resistance is widespread among malaria-carrying mosquitoes in Nigeria, reducing how effectively pyrethroid-only mosquito nets kill mosquitoes that land on them. Pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets, a type of dual active ingredient LLIN, add chlorfenapyr, an insecticide that kills mosquitoes through a different biological mechanism. WHO strongly recommends these nets over pyrethroid-only nets in areas with pyrethroid resistance (WHO, 2023).

How far has resistance gone? At one Jigawa surveillance site in 2017, a standard dose of deltamethrin killed 1% of exposed Anopheles coluzzii. Eight years earlier, it killed 78% (Ibrahim et al., 2019).

This guide covers the Nigerian resistance evidence, how chlorfenapyr nets work, the trial results behind them, what WHO recommends, how long they last, which products are prequalified, and who manufactures them in Nigeria. Every figure links to its primary source.

Disclosure: Harvestfield Healthcare, the publisher of this guide, manufactures Synera DuoForte, one of the six products compared below. Competing products are covered to the same evidence standard.

Pyrethroid resistance in Nigeria: the short version

  • Pyrethroid resistance is widespread among Nigerian malaria vectors, though levels vary sharply between locations.

  • At some northern surveillance sites, standard pyrethroid doses have killed fewer than 1 in 5 mosquitoes.

  • Chlorfenapyr kills by disrupting the mosquito's energy supply, not its nervous system, so common pyrethroid-resistance mechanisms do not give the same protection against it.

  • Large trials in Tanzania and Benin found substantial reductions in malaria compared with pyrethroid-only nets, including a 46% reduction in infections among children in Benin.

  • WHO strongly recommends pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets over pyrethroid-only nets where resistance is present.

  • Six pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets are WHO-prequalified, and two are now manufactured in Nigeria.

What is pyrethroid resistance?

Pyrethroid resistance means a mosquito population survives doses of pyrethroid insecticide that would once have killed it. WHO classes a population as resistant when fewer than 90% of mosquitoes die in a standard susceptibility test.

The mosquitoes are resistant to the insecticide, not to the net. An intact net still blocks bites as a physical barrier. What resistance removes is the net's ability to kill mosquitoes that land on it, which is what protects the wider community and not just the person underneath.

How widespread is pyrethroid resistance in Nigeria?

Published surveillance shows widespread pyrethroid resistance across Nigerian malaria-vector populations, although resistance levels vary considerably between locations. A 2025 review of 54 studies across 180 locations found pyrethroids to be the most-resisted insecticide class, with pockets of susceptibility only in limited parts of Lagos, Ondo and Delta states (Adeogun et al., 2025).

WHO's resistance threshold is 90% mortality. Below it, a population is classed as resistant.

Resistance is also getting worse where it has been tracked over time. At the Jigawa site, deltamethrin mortality fell from 78% in 2009 to 1% in 2017 (Ibrahim et al., 2019).

A caveat on the data: state coverage is uneven, sites were sampled in different years, and a single LGA does not represent a whole state. The direction of travel is consistent across studies, though.

Why are Nigerian mosquitoes becoming resistant to pyrethroids?

Two mechanisms account for most of it, and many Nigerian populations carry both.

  • Metabolic resistance. Mosquitoes over-produce cytochrome P450 enzymes that break pyrethroids down before they act. Lagos and Ogun populations showed the highest resistance intensity, linked to elevated P450 and GST enzymes (Awolola et al., 2018). National surveillance found the same enzyme-driven pattern across 12 states (Adeogun et al., 2026).

  • Target-site resistance. The kdr mutation changes the nerve channel pyrethroids attack, blunting their effect. It occurs at every surveyed site. In Kwara, 41.6% of genotyped mosquitoes carried two resistant copies (Iyiola et al., 2026).

The dominant vector matters too. An. coluzzii made up 79.8% of collections in the 2020–2024 national survey (Adeogun et al., 2026), and it is the species behind the most extreme northern results.

The metabolic mechanism is the key to the next section. Some of the enzymes that protect mosquitoes from pyrethroids are also involved in making chlorfenapyr toxic.

What is chlorfenapyr?

Chlorfenapyr is an insecticide from the pyrrole class. Pyrethroids attack the mosquito's nervous system; chlorfenapyr disrupts how its cells produce energy. Because chlorfenapyr acts through a different biological mechanism, common pyrethroid-resistance mechanisms do not confer the same protection against it.

It is not a stronger dose of the same idea. It is a separate way of killing.

How do chlorfenapyr mosquito nets work?

A pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr net carries both insecticides on the same fabric. A mosquito that contacts the net is exposed to two insecticides with different modes of action, giving the net an additional killing mechanism where pyrethroid resistance is present.

Why P450 resistance matters

Chlorfenapyr has to be activated inside the mosquito before it becomes toxic, and some of the enzymes linked to pyrethroid resistance take part in that activation.

At the molecular level, chlorfenapyr is a pro-insecticide. P450 enzymes strip off its N-ethoxymethyl group, turning it into tralopyril. Tralopyril uncouples the mitochondrial proton gradient that cells use to make ATP (Yunta et al., 2023). The activating enzymes include CYP6P3 and CYP9K1, both associated with pyrethroid resistance in An. gambiae. Some P450 enzymes associated with pyrethroid resistance can therefore also activate chlorfenapyr, which may help explain why pyrethroid-resistant populations can remain susceptible to it (Yunta et al., 2023).

In testing across 16 African countries, including three Nigerian sites, wild An. gambiae with multiple pyrethroid-resistance mechanisms remained susceptible to chlorfenapyr (Oxborough et al., 2021).

Why keep the pyrethroid?

The pyrethroid still repels some mosquitoes, kills the susceptible fraction quickly, and gives the net a second route to a kill. The two insecticides work as a mixture, not as backups for each other.

Why lab tests can understate chlorfenapyr

Chlorfenapyr works best on active mosquitoes because its toxicity depends on the insect's metabolism. Standard three-minute cone tests produce very low mortality, and raising the test temperature from 22°C to 27°C increased the odds of mortality about 41-fold. Overnight tunnel tests with host-seeking mosquitoes are the reliable measure (Oxborough et al., 2015). Product comparisons based on cone tests alone will mislead.

Can mosquitoes become resistant to chlorfenapyr?

Yes, in principle. Reduced chlorfenapyr susceptibility has already been recorded in An. gambiae from Cameroon, Ghana and the DRC, with bottle-assay mortality as low as 64% (Tchouakui et al., 2023). No such result has been published for Nigeria, but routine monitoring is the only way to know.

Do chlorfenapyr mosquito nets work against resistant mosquitoes?

Yes. Two large cluster-randomised trials, both using Interceptor G2, found clear reductions in malaria compared with pyrethroid-only nets:

  • Tanzania: over 39,000 households; the nets nearly halved malaria cases over two years.

  • Benin: 54,000 households; the nets reduced malaria infections in children aged six months to 10 years by 46%.

Source: LSHTM, 2023.

Across trials and pilot deployments, dual-insecticide nets improved malaria control by 20–50% compared with pyrethroid-only nets (WHO). No equivalent trial has been run in Nigeria; the evidence comes from West and East African settings with similar resistance profiles.

What does WHO recommend?

WHO has recommended pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets since March 2023, and the recommendation is specific about where they apply and what they replace.

The conditions attached matter as much as the headline:

  • Coverage comes first. Programmes should confirm they can cover the extra cost of dual active ingredient nets while keeping optimal coverage (WHO Guidelines for malaria, 2023). A household with a pyrethroid-only net is better protected than one with no net.

  • Use prequalified products. The recommendation applies to WHO-prequalified nets.

  • Match nets to local resistance. WHO asks programmes to consider local resistance mechanisms when targeting deployment. Nigerian surveillance already shows P450-driven resistance in most sampled states, the profile where chlorfenapyr is expected to perform well.

  • Monitor chlorfenapyr itself. In June 2026, WHO clarified that a population counts as susceptible to chlorfenapyr when bioassay mortality is at least 98% (WHO, 11 June 2026). Nigerian surveillance sites should add chlorfenapyr testing as these nets roll out.

Adoption has moved fast. Dual-insecticide nets made up nearly 80% of nets delivered in sub-Saharan Africa in 2023, up from 59% in 2022 (WHO).

How long do chlorfenapyr mosquito nets last?

The "three years" attached to long-lasting insecticidal nets is a design standard, not a household guarantee. WHO defines an LLIN as one expected to keep its biological activity for "at least 20 standard WHO washes under laboratory conditions and 3 years of recommended use under field conditions" (WHO, 2011). A washed net passes if it still kills at least 80% of test mosquitoes (or meets knockdown or blood-feeding thresholds).

Field evidence for dual active ingredient nets is more mixed:

  • Chlorfenapyr is lost faster in homes than in the lab. Interceptor G2 nets from Tanzanian households kept only 8% of their original chlorfenapyr after 36 months, against 32–37% for laboratory-washed nets. Their advantage over pyrethroid-only nets in experimental huts was significant at 12 months (43% vs 21% mortality) but not at 24 or 36 months (Martin et al., 2024).

  • The same nets still reduced malaria for three years. The linked trial found the public-health benefit held over the full three years. Why is not settled; one hypothesis is an added effect of chlorfenapyr on parasite development (Martin et al., 2024).

WHO itself notes that "the assumption of a uniform 3-year lifespan may be over-optimistic" and that durability varies by location, household and net (WHO, 2011). A three-year label means a product passed a standard. It does not say how long a net will work in a given Nigerian household, and Nigerian field-durability studies have not yet been published.

Which pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets are WHO-prequalified?

WHO prequalification is the assessment of a product's quality, safety and efficacy that makes it eligible for procurement by most international malaria programmes. Six pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets hold it as of September 2026. They differ in the pyrethroid partner, the insecticide loading and the evidence behind them, not in how chlorfenapyr works.

Interceptor G2: the reference product

Interceptor G2 was the first net in the class. It was used in the Tanzania and Benin trials that underpin WHO's recommendation, so most of what is known about the class in real communities comes from it. Its field durability limits are also the best documented.

Synera DuoForte vs Interceptor G2: same actives, higher pyrethroid load

Synera DuoForte, the alpha-cypermethrin and chlorfenapyr net from GDM Health Products, uses the same two active ingredients as Interceptor G2. Its alpha-cypermethrin content (3.75 g/kg) is above Interceptor G2's specified range; its chlorfenapyr content (5.6 g/kg) sits within it.

In WHO's prequalification assessment, Synera DuoForte washed 20 times was non-inferior and superior to an Interceptor G2-equivalent net in experimental huts in Benin and Tanzania, and superior to a pyrethroid-only net (WHO public assessment report, part 5). Like every product except Interceptor G2, it has no cluster-randomised trial of its own; its prequalification relies on experimental-hut non-inferiority against the reference product.

PermaNet Dual vs Interceptor G2: a different pyrethroid partner

PermaNet Dual uses deltamethrin instead of alpha-cypermethrin, at a lower pyrethroid load (84 mg/m²), with the same chlorfenapyr load as Interceptor G2 (200 mg/m²). In Benin experimental huts it was non-inferior to Interceptor G2 for mosquito mortality after 20 washes (75% each) and outperformed a pyrethroid-PBO net (Syme et al., 2023).

What the differences mean in practice

  • Chlorfenapyr loadings are similar across the class, clustering around 200 mg/m², with PRONet Duo higher. Where pyrethroid resistance is intense, the choice of pyrethroid partner is unlikely to be decisive.

  • Hut mortality figures are not comparable across studies. Compare products only within the same trial.

  • Only Interceptor G2 has epidemiological trial data. For the others, WHO treats hut-trial non-inferiority to Interceptor G2 as sufficient evidence of comparable public-health impact.

Local production changes lead times, foreign-exchange exposure and supply security for a country that carries roughly a quarter of the world's malaria cases. It does not change the science: a net made in Ogun or Lagos has to meet the same prequalification specification as one made in China or Vietnam.

What this means for malaria control in Nigeria

For programme managers, procurement agencies and journalists, four questions are worth asking of any dual active ingredient LLIN, local or imported:

  1. Is this manufacturing site listed under the product's WHO prequalification? Prequalification covers a product made at named sites. Check the WHO dossier and the Global Fund's list of eligible sites, not just the product name.

  2. What does local surveillance say? State-level resistance data should guide where dual active ingredient nets go first, especially where P450-driven resistance is documented.

  3. Is chlorfenapyr susceptibility being monitored? No Nigerian reduction has been published, but monitoring needs to start before wide deployment, not after.

  4. Is anyone measuring field durability in Nigeria? The three-year figure is a laboratory proxy. Nigerian households, washing habits and climate may produce different results.

The open research questions are Nigerian field-durability data for each product, chlorfenapyr susceptibility baselines by state, and whether hut-trial non-inferiority holds up epidemiologically for products other than Interceptor G2.

The bottom line

Pyrethroid resistance has changed what effective malaria vector control requires in Nigeria. Chlorfenapyr nets do not solve every operational problem, but they add a second mode of action where pyrethroid-only nets are losing effectiveness. The priorities now are to match deployment to local resistance data, maintain high coverage, monitor chlorfenapyr susceptibility, and build Nigerian evidence on field durability.

Frequently asked questions

Are mosquitoes in Nigeria resistant to mosquito nets?

No. They are resistant to pyrethroid insecticides, not to the net itself. An intact net still blocks bites. Resistance reduces how many mosquitoes the net kills, which weakens the protection it gives the wider community.

What is a chlorfenapyr net?

A chlorfenapyr net is a long-lasting insecticidal net treated with a pyrethroid plus chlorfenapyr, an insecticide that kills by disrupting the mosquito's energy production. It is designed for areas where mosquitoes survive pyrethroids.

Why does chlorfenapyr work when pyrethroids do not?

Pyrethroids act on the mosquito's nerves, and many Nigerian mosquitoes now carry enzymes and nerve mutations that blunt them. Chlorfenapyr attacks the cells' energy supply instead, and some of those same resistance enzymes help activate it.

What is a dual active ingredient LLIN?

A dual active ingredient LLIN carries two active ingredients instead of one pyrethroid. The second ingredient is either another insecticide (chlorfenapyr), an insect growth regulator (pyriproxyfen), or, in a related category, a synergist (PBO) that blocks resistance enzymes.

Does WHO recommend chlorfenapyr mosquito nets?

Yes. Since March 2023, WHO has strongly recommended pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets over pyrethroid-only nets in areas with pyrethroid resistance.

Are chlorfenapyr mosquito nets manufactured in Nigeria?

Yes. Since September 2026, Harvestfield Healthcare FZE in Ogun State produces Synera DuoForte, and Health Textiles Nigeria FZE in Lagos produces PermaNet Dual.

How long do insecticide-treated mosquito nets last?

WHO's standard for long-lasting nets is 20 laboratory washes and three years of recommended field use. Real-world lifespan varies by household, and chlorfenapyr content can fall faster in homes than in laboratory tests.
